Name: strategy_affordance_mismatch
Title: Wrong Tool for the Job: Overthinking as a Strategy-Selection Mismatch Between the Problem's Afforded Solution Method and the One the Model Executes
Short Hypothesis: Reasoning models pre-encode, before generating any reasoning token, a linearly-decodable 'strategy affordance' signal indicating which class of solution method a problem invites (e.g., direct recall/formula-application vs. multi-step derivation vs. case-enumeration). A large slice of overthinking is a strategy mismatch: the model executes a heavier strategy than the problem affords. This mismatch predicts wasted tokens better than a scalar difficulty or success probe, and steering the model toward the afforded (cheaper) strategy at problem onset cuts tokens without hurting accuracy.
Related Work: Prior efficient-reasoning interpretability reads a scalar pre-generation signal and allocates a length/compute budget from it: LLMs Encode Their Failures (2026) and difficulty-perception probes predict model-specific difficulty for routing; Temporal Predictors of Outcome (2025) and Knowing Before Saying (2025) probe eventual correctness early; Tracing the Traces (2025) uses latent-trajectory signals to pick promising traces; FR-Ponder / Learning to Ponder (2025) learn instance-adaptive scalar compute; Efficiency Steering / ReflCtrl (2025) steer a single verbosity/reflection direction. Crucially all treat the pre-generation signal as one-dimensional (how hard / how likely to succeed / how long) and control a scalar knob (budget, length, reflection). A separate line (Behavior and Representation in LLMs for Combinatorial Optimization, 2025) shows hidden states support per-instance ALGORITHM selection, but for external solver choice, not for the model's own reasoning, and offers no efficiency intervention. Our proposal is distinct and is directly inspired by cognitive neuroscience findings that the brain decides *whether* to engage costly forward planning via a fast planning-value proxy (ACC, 2021) and shifts from rule-based to memory-based processing via cost-benefit analysis (2025): we claim reasoning models carry a multi-class strategy-affordance representation, that overthinking is a *mismatch* between afforded and executed strategy (not merely a mis-set scalar budget), and that steering toward the afforded strategy is an interpretable efficiency fix. This is a strategy-selection account, orthogonal to all my prior overthinking proposals (which concern answer-commitment, verification, length priors, etc.) and to scalar difficulty/budget work.
Abstract: Reasoning language models overthink, and prior interpretability work explains this via a scalar internal signal (difficulty, success-likelihood, or a verbosity direction) that sets how *much* to think. We propose a categorical account inspired by human cognitive control: before generating any reasoning token, a model encodes a strategy-affordance signal indicating *which kind* of solution method a problem invites—direct recall/formula-application, multi-step algebraic derivation, or case-enumeration/search. We hypothesize that a large share of overthinking is a strategy mismatch: the model executes a heavier strategy than the problem affords (e.g., laboriously deriving what could be recalled, or enumerating what a formula solves in one line). Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we (1) label each problem's afforded strategy and each trace's executed strategy via lightweight parsing plus LLM-judge; (2) train linear probes on the prompt-boundary residual stream to decode afforded strategy and test separability from a scalar difficulty probe; (3) show a mismatch metric (afforded-cheap but executed-heavy) predicts wasted tokens better than difficulty or success probes; (4) localize the strategy-affordance representation and causally validate it via activation patching (patch a cheap-strategy affordance into a heavy-strategy context and observe strategy switch); and (5) build a training-free intervention that steers the model toward the afforded strategy at onset, cutting tokens at equal accuracy versus scalar length steering and difficulty budgeting. Our work reframes a slice of overthinking as picking the wrong solution method and gives it an identifiable, steerable internal cause.
Experiments: 1) Strategy taxonomy and labeling: Define a small, model-agnostic set of solution-strategy classes appropriate to math/science reasoning (e.g., DIRECT-RECALL/formula-application, MULTI-STEP-DERIVATION, CASE-ENUMERATION/search, ELIMINATION for MCQ). For each problem, label the AFFORDED strategy = the cheapest strategy that yields the correct answer, obtained by prompting the model (and an independent LLM-judge) to produce a minimal correct solution and classifying it, cross-checked with a reference minimal solution where available. For each generated reasoning trace, label the EXECUTED strategy via parsing (equation vs case-split vs recall patterns) plus LLM-judge. Validate labels with human spot-checks; report inter-rater agreement. 2) Prevalence of mismatch: Compute the executed-vs-afforded confusion matrix per dataset/model size; quantify the fraction of traces where executed strategy is strictly heavier than afforded, and the token overhead of these traces relative to matched afforded-strategy traces (via truncate-and-resume minimal-solve length and via forcing the afforded strategy by prompt). Show mismatch is a substantial, distinct source of waste. 3) Strategy-affordance probing (Location): At the prompt boundary (last prompt token, before any reasoning token), extract residual-stream activations and train a multi-class linear probe to predict the afforded strategy. Metrics: macro-F1/accuracy, layer sweep. Baselines for separability: (a) a scalar difficulty probe (trained on pass-rate), (b) a success-likelihood probe, (c) surface features (length, TF-IDF). Test whether afforded strategy is decodable above and beyond difficulty (principal angles between strategy directions and the difficulty direction; predictive gain in a joint model). 4) Mismatch predicts waste: Define a mismatch score from (probe-afforded strategy) vs (realized executed strategy). Regress wasted tokens (tokens beyond the minimal-solve length via truncate-and-resume) on the mismatch score vs. baselines (difficulty probe, success probe, trace length); compare R^2. 5) Causal validation (Causal Intervention): Use activation patching to identify layers/components carrying the strategy-affordance signal; patch the prompt-boundary state from a cheap-strategy-affording problem into a heavy-strategy context (same target answer/method family where constructible) and test whether the executed strategy switches toward the cheaper one (strategy-class change + token drop). Controls: matched-random-direction patch; off-target accuracy preserved; report sign, dose, specificity. 6) Training-free intervention: Derive a strategy-steering direction (difference-of-means between cheap-strategy and heavy-strategy affordance activations) and, when the probe predicts a cheap strategy is afforded, steer at problem onset to induce it. Evaluate on GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, GPQA. Baselines: no intervention, scalar length/verbosity steering (Efficiency Steering), difficulty-budgeting (FR-Ponder-style), fixed truncation, and prompting ('use the simplest method'). Metrics: accuracy (overall and hardest strata), mean tokens, tokens-at-equal-accuracy, wall-clock speedup, and strategy-switch rate. Key claim: strategy steering Pareto-dominates scalar length steering because it targets the specific waste (wrong method) rather than blunt shortening. 7) Failure/safety analysis: verify steering toward a cheap strategy does NOT fire on problems that genuinely require a heavy strategy (specificity: measure underthinking / accuracy drop on truly heavy-afforded items as a function of probe confidence). 8) Generalization: transfer probe and steering direction across datasets and model scales without retraining.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The strategy taxonomy may be fuzzy—some problems admit no single 'afforded' strategy, and labels from LLM-judge/parsing are noisy; we mitigate with a small, coarse class set, human validation, and reporting agreement, and treat ambiguous cases separately. The afforded-strategy signal may be inseparable from scalar difficulty (harder problems simply afford heavier strategies), which would collapse our account into existing difficulty-budgeting work—the separability analysis, joint-model predictive-gain test, and causal patching directly address this, and a null separability result is itself an informative finding. Constructing patching pairs that hold the answer/method fixed while flipping afforded strategy is nontrivial; we use templated problem variants and report where clean pairs are unavailable. Steering toward a cheaper strategy could cause underthinking on problems that truly need a heavy method (accuracy loss); the specificity/hardest-strata analysis and confidence gating quantify this trade-off. Minimal-solve-length estimation via truncate-and-resume is compute-heavy and noisy; we subsample. Intervention gains may not exceed strong scalar steering on tokens alone, but the mechanistic reframing (overthinking as strategy mismatch with a decodable, steerable affordance representation) is a standalone contribution. Effects are likely model-family and scale specific, and afforded-strategy structure may differ across domains.
